ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The image shows electron shell diagrams arranged by columns for Group 1, Group 14, Group 17, and Group 18, and by rows for Period 1, Period 2, and Period 3. In the Group 1 column, H, Li, and Na can be seen, and their outermost shells show 1 electron; in the Group 14 column, the outermost shells of C and Si show 4 electrons; in the Group 17 column, the outermost shells of F and Cl show 7 electrons; in the Group 18 column, the outer shells of He, Ne, and Ar are full. Reasoning: Strong ionic bonds usually form between atoms that easily lose electrons and atoms that easily gain electrons. Group 1 atoms have only 1 valence electron and easily lose this electron to form positive ions; Group 17 atoms have 7 valence electrons and easily gain 1 electron to fill the outer shell and form negative ions. Therefore, these two ions with opposite charges will strongly attract each other, forming a strong ionic bond.

raw_record.question_text: Using the figure, which two groups will form a strong ionic bond?

method.method_draft: First describe the figure: it shows electron-shell diagrams organized by group and period, including Group 1, Group 14, Group 17, and Group 18. Compare the outermost electrons in each group. Group 1 atoms have a single valence electron, making them likely to give it away. Group 17 atoms have seven valence electrons, making them likely to accept one electron to complete their outer shell. Since ionic bonding is strongest between an electron donor and an electron acceptor, select Group 1 and Group 17.
method.CoT_raw: 图像描述：图中按列显示了 Group 1、Group 14、Group 17 和 Group 18，按行显示 Period 1、Period 2、Period 3 的电子层示意图。Group 1 列中可见 H、Li、Na，它们最外层显示 1 个电子；Group 14 列中 C、Si 最外层显示 4 个电子；Group 17 列中 F、Cl 最外层显示 7 个电子；Group 18 列中 He、Ne、Ar 外层已满。推理：强离子键通常形成于容易失去电子的原子和容易得到电子的原子之间。Group 1 原子只有 1 个价电子，容易失去该电子形成正离子；Group 17 原子有 7 个价电子，容易得到 1 个电子补满外层形成负离子。因此，这两个带相反电荷的离子会强烈相互吸引，形成强离子键。

planner_metadata.distinctiveness_rationale: This is the direct valence-electron route: it uses the outer-shell electron counts shown in the Bohr-style group columns to identify the best electron donor and acceptor. The problem has essentially one natural solution, so this single method is sufficient.
planner_metadata.image_role: Read the figure as a periodic-group comparison with columns labeled Group 1, Group 14, Group 17, and Group 18. Note that Group 1 examples such as Li and Na show one electron in the outer shell, while Group 17 examples such as F and Cl show seven outer-shell electrons, one short of a full shell. Group 18 examples already have full outer shells.
planner_metadata.text_role: Use the question text to determine that the requested output is the pair of groups, not specific elements, that would form a strong ionic bond.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: Use the rule that a strong ionic bond forms when one atom readily loses an electron and another readily gains it, producing oppositely charged ions with stable full valence shells. Group 1 atoms tend to lose one electron; Group 17 atoms tend to gain one electron.
